statement: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's highest temperature reached 31.1 °C (88 °F) (146 of 1,095 days, here called hot days), compared with other days, were associated with more deaths certified by the city's medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose: 2.34 a day against 1.76 (341 deaths on hot days, 1,667 on other days), a third more (Marzuk et al., 1998); by the editors' calculation a rate ratio of 1.33 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.49), or about 85 deaths more than the other-day rate predicts, some 4 in 100 of the 2,008 cocaine overdose deaths of those three years. The days were compared without any adjustment for season, day of the week, holidays or trend, and nobody's heat exposure, amount used or pattern of use was known. Deaths from opiates without cocaine were 0.81 against 0.71 a day and other overdose deaths 0.08 on both kinds of day, neither difference significant, but by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio (1.14, 0.93 to 1.38) did not differ significantly from the cocaine one (ratio of the two 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47), so the paper's reading that the rise was specific to cocaine is not established; the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in their blood was much the same on hot and other days (18.9 against 19.5 in 100; 9.5 against 10.3 in 100), which the authors read as cocaine use not rising on hot days; and opiates were also found in about 6 in 10 of the deaths counted as cocaine overdoses. The temperature threshold was chosen from the 1990 to 1992 overdose deaths and the dates of heat deaths with cocaine, then tested on the 1993 to 1995 deaths; of 40 tested deaths certified as due to overheating (hyperthermia) in 1990 to 1995, 10 had a breakdown product of cocaine in the body. In a laboratory experiment (Crandall et al., 2002), 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine were heated at rest in a suit carrying water at 46 °C after one intranasal dose of cocaine (2 mg per kg, described by the authors as low; study conditions) and, on another day in random order, after the same dose of lidocaine, a local anaesthetic used as the comparison (called placebo in the abstract): before heating, core temperature did not differ (36.79 against 36.75 °C), but during heating it rose more after cocaine (P < 0.001; to about 37.8 against 37.5 °C after about 38 minutes, read from the paper's figure and approximate); the skin's blood vessels began to widen, and sweating began, at a core temperature about 0.3 °C higher (37.37 against 37.06 °C and 37.38 against 37.07 °C; by the editors' calculation, 95% CIs of about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C); at a core temperature of 37.86 °C, skin blood flow was 49 against 70 in 100 of its maximum and sweat rate 0.8 against 1.0 mg per cm² per minute (how many people reached that temperature is not stated); and people felt less hot at the same core temperature. Heat production was not measured, so the authors' conclusion that cocaine raises body temperature mainly by impairing heat loss is an inference; they expect larger doses to add heat production, say the results may not apply to people who use cocaine regularly, and did not test their suggestion that hot weather and crowded clubs amplify the effect. Neither study followed people who used cocaine in hot weather. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In New York City in the 1990s, hot days had about a third more deaths recorded as cocaine overdoses than other days (2.34 against 1.76 a day). The days were compared without allowing for season or anything else that comes with summer, and the study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine. In a laboratory, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were heated after one small dose: their skin began to flush and sweat only at a higher body temperature, their body temperature rose more than after a comparison drug, and they felt less hot. Neither study looked at people using cocaine in hot weather.

risk_of_bias.note: Day comparison (card sc_marzuk_1998): ROBINS-E high, entirely unadjusted (season, day of week, holidays and trend not modelled); deaths counted through the medical examiner's certification; the negative-control comparisons are imprecise and were not compared with the cocaine estimate. Laboratory study (card sc_crandall_2002): RoB 2 some concerns (how the order was randomized not reported; blinding not checked although cocaine raised heart rate and blood pressure, which matters for the felt heat; number contributing at the highest temperatures unknown; no protocol; about 22 comparisons without correction).

inconsistency.note: The two studies answer different parts of the question (deaths on hot days; heat-loss responses in the laboratory), and no replication of either was read.

indirectness.note: One city in 1993 to 1995 and counts of deaths per day, not anyone's own heat exposure or use; the laboratory study gave one low intranasal dose to 7 people who had never used cocaine, heated passively at rest, unlike use outside the laboratory (larger or repeated amounts, exertion, other drugs).

imprecision.note: Seven people in the laboratory, with the intervals for the comparisons at 37.86 °C close to no difference; the opiate comparison cannot exclude a rise of about a third. The cocaine rate ratio itself is precise (1.18 to 1.49).

large_effect.note: Not applied: a rate ratio of 1.33 from an unadjusted comparison.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the paper's 'steady increase' above the threshold rests on cumulative and moving-average curves without a test of trend (card reporting issues).

grade.reasoning: The day comparison is observational and starts low; rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, it is very low. The laboratory study, rated alone, would start high as a randomized crossover and be rated down for risk of bias, indirectness (one low dose in people who had never used cocaine, at rest) and imprecision (7 people), also very low. 'Is associated with': the death counts come from an unadjusted comparison of days, and the laboratory study shows what one dose did to heat-loss responses under passive heating, not what happens to people who use cocaine in hot weather. Status single study: each part rests on one study; the laboratory study is consistent with the death counts but does not replicate them, and it takes them as its starting point. Not read: the editorial on the New York study (Kilbourne, 1998), the published letter on the laboratory study with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002), a later study of the same association (Auger et al., 2017) and population studies of heat and drug deaths on the reading list. The post-mortem cocaine levels that the laboratory paper's introduction cites are second-hand and not used.

statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, from a PubMed search to October 2019 run mainly by one author) tabulates 52 published cases from 1991 to 2018, 21 of them deaths, with sodium of 101 to 130 mmol/L in the 36 rows that give one, but its table has errors: it appears to list two patients twice, cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one case, includes three deaths with no low sodium recorded, leaves one death's outcome blank and draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series, so it adds no independent count. The amount taken is unknown or blank in 30 of its 52 rows, although that review, like the earlier one, says most cases followed a single dose; and in its 10 deaths with a sodium value, sodium (109 to 126 mmol/L) lay within the range of those who recovered (editors' count). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review cites no study that measured how much people drank, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).
plain: After MDMA, some young people have been treated in hospital because the salt (sodium) in their blood fell too low, causing fits and swelling of the brain. It started within hours of taking MDMA. In a UK group of 17 people aged 15 to 26, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid, and two died: both had taken one tablet, had been drinking a lot of water, and drank or were given more water after they felt ill. In California, 73 of 188 people who had their sodium measured had a low level, and 4 of them died. These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens. Most of the UK group had taken one or two tablets, and no study has compared amounts. The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water; that part is not proven.
population: Mostly young people who became ill after taking ecstasy (MDMA) and came to a poison service or hospital: 17 patients aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (1993 to 1996); 545 poison-centre cases in California in 2000 to 2005 (mean age 21), 188 of them with a measured sodium; and published case reports as described in two narrative reviews (more than 25 reports to 2008; 52 tabulated cases to 2018, with errors)
exposure: MDMA sold as ecstasy tablets, content unknown (MDMA confirmed by laboratory tests in 8 of the 15 UK survivors and in both who died; in California by history, with urine screens in 103 of 188 and no specific method), with fluid intake recorded only for some: a large amount in 10 of the 17 UK patients; stated amounts of half a tablet to three tablets in 13 UK survivors; one published case took five tablets (study conditions as reported, not recommendations)
comparator: None for the UK series and the case reports; in California, cases with a sodium of 130 mmol/L or more or reported as normal (115 of 188)
outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L, seizures, coma, brain swelling, death, and the temperature recorded at hospital
magnitude: UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: Table 3, 52 rows 1991–2018 (editors' count: 46 women, 21 deaths, 27 recoveries; sodium 101–130 mmol/L in 36 rows, 109–126 in the 10 deaths with a value; amount unknown or blank in 30 rows), with probable duplicates (about 50 distinct cases), an untraceable citation, 3 fatal rows without recorded low sodium and 10 deaths from the California series. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.

grade.reasoning: Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken. The only comparison read of women and men given the same amount is described second-hand in a 2020 narrative review (Faria et al., 2020): in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women were given 125 mg of MDMA in a laboratory (study conditions), and copeptin, a marker of the water-holding hormone, rose in the women but not in the men, while no significant differences were seen in the hormone itself or in blood sodium. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent; the 2020 review's table of published cases (1991 to 2018) lists 46 women among 52 rows (the review's 89 in 100), from which it infers that women are predisposed, but the table appears to count two patients twice (44 of 50, 88 in 100, editors' calculation), cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one woman's case, draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series and sets no case count against the number of women and men who take MDMA. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the reviews offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested in people who took MDMA; the 2020 review's main support for a greater risk to women once the brain swells comes from patients after surgery, among whom women who still menstruated were about 25 times more likely than men or women past menopause to die or have lasting brain injury (Ayus et al., 1992, as described in the review).
plain: In California poison-centre records, women with MDMA illness were more likely than men to have a low level of blood sodium: 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) against 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), among those who had their sodium measured. Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma. The reports count people who became ill and were reported, not everyone who took MDMA, and sodium was measured in about a third of them, so this does not show how likely low sodium is in women or men who take MDMA. In the one small laboratory study that gave 8 women and 8 men the same amount, a review reports no clear differences in the water-holding hormone or in blood sodium, although a marker of the hormone rose only in the women. These were mostly young people (average age 21).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical on the card: the people are those who were reported and tested (spectrum and referral bias), sodium was recorded in about a third, the odds ratios are unadjusted for body weight, amount of MDMA, fluid intake or other drugs, and exposure is by history.

inconsistency.note: The UK series and the two reviews' case tables point the same way, though they are descriptions without a test and the tables overlap the California series. The one controlled laboratory comparison of the sexes, described second-hand, found no significant difference in the water-holding hormone or in sodium; it bears on susceptibility at a fixed laboratory dose, not on who was found among reported cases, so it qualifies the claim rather than contradicting it.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who became ill and were reported, which is what was studied.

imprecision.note: The main interval (2.08 to 7.59) excludes 1 but is wide; the within-sex odds ratios for coma and seizure have intervals up to 12.90 and 7.07.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the odds ratio (about 4) is large, but the people studied are those reported and tested, and unmeasured differences in body weight, amount taken and fluid drunk could produce or hide it (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: One poison-centre case series with a comparison inside it starts low (observational). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors themselves say causality cannot be determined, and sex is bound up with body size, amount taken and fluid drunk, none of which was recorded. Status single study: only the California series tests the sex difference among reported cases; the UK series and the two reviews are consistent but do not test it, and both reviews' tables overlap the California series. The 2020 review (Faria et al.; card sc_faria_2020) infers a female predisposition from its case counts, but its table has errors and no denominators, and the only controlled comparison it describes (Simmler et al., 2011, not read) found no significant difference in the hormone or in sodium; that study and the postoperative data (Ayus et al., 1992, not read) are second-hand. The answer to who is most at risk cannot be read from this claim: it gives who was found among reported cases with a sodium result, not who is at risk among people who take MDMA, and no age comparison is possible.
